specPoints.text: understand that potassium dichromate(VI) in dilute sulfuric acid can oxidise: i primary alcohols to produce aldehydes (which give a positive result with Benedict’s or Fehling’s solution) if the product is distilled as it forms ii primary alcohols to produce carboxylic acids (which give a positive result with sodium carbonate or sodium hydrogencarbonate) if the reagents are heated under reflux iii secondary alcohols to produce ketones In equations, the oxidising agent can be represented by [O].

primer.text: Acidified dichromate turns an alcohol's class into its oxidation ceiling. This note follows primary alcohols to aldehydes and acids, secondary ones to ketones, and tertiary ones nowhere, reads the orange-to-green shift, then matches Fehling's and Tollens' tests and the two apparatus choices to the target product.

lessons.title: Dichromate oxidation and the three alcohol classes
lessons.opening: Acidified potassium dichromate(VI) is the workhorse oxidising agent for alcohols, and the alcohol class decides how far oxidation runs. This lesson ties primary to aldehydes and acids, secondary to ketones, tertiary to nothing, and reads the orange-to-green colour change as the reaction's report card.
keyPoints: Primary alcohols oxidise to aldehydes, which oxidise further to carboxylic acids.
Secondary alcohols oxidise to ketones only, and tertiary alcohols resist oxidation altogether.
Acidified potassium dichromate(VI) is orange, and it oxidises alcohols while being reduced to green Cr3+ ions.
Acidified means the dichromate sits in dilute acid, supplying the H+ ions the reduction demands.
The aldehyde boils lower than its parent alcohol, so it can be distilled off as it forms to stop at that stage.

low.restatement: Warm the alcohol with orange acidified dichromate: primary alcohols climb two rungs to aldehyde then acid unless the aldehyde is distilled away, secondary alcohols stop at the ketone, and tertiary alcohols never leave base camp, while the reagent turns green as it works.
low.analogy: A climbing wall where every route ends at a different height: primary routes reach two platforms, secondary routes one, and tertiary routes are closed at the door.
low.examPointer: Quote the colour change orange to green as evidence of oxidation, and name the product class for each alcohol class.

medium.restatement: Dichromate reduction consumes hydrogen ions, which the dilute acid supplies; the alcohol hands over hydrogens and electrons, the chromium drops from +6 to +3, and the visible green shift certifies that oxidation truly occurred rather than merely heating.
medium.analogy: The orange reagent is a taxi fleet that only moves passengers when it can itself take on fuel in the form of hydrogen ions from the acid.
medium.examPointer: Explain why tertiary alcohols fail the test by referencing the missing hydrogen on the carbinol carbon when required.

check.stem: What colour change shows that acidified dichromate has oxidised an alcohol?

options.text: Orange to green, as Cr2O7 2- is reduced to Cr3+
options.explanation: The oxidising agent turns from orange dichromate to green chromium(III) as it works.

options.text: Green to orange, as the chromium gains electrons
options.explanation: The change runs the other way; oxidation of the alcohol reduces the chromium.

options.text: Colourless to pink
options.explanation: That describes an indicator, not dichromate.

options.text: No colour change ever occurs
options.explanation: The orange-to-green shift is the standard observable.

check.stem: Why must potassium dichromate be acidified to act as an oxidising agent?

options.text: Its reduction requires hydrogen ions, which the dilute acid supplies
options.explanation: The Cr2O7 2- to Cr3+ reduction consumes H+, so the acidic medium is a chemical requirement.

options.text: The acid makes the solution orange so the colour change is visible
options.explanation: Dichromate is orange before acidification plays any role.

options.text: The acid catalyses the alcohol's dehydration instead
options.explanation: The acid enables the dichromate's own reduction, not dehydration.

options.text: Acid prevents the alcohol from evaporating
options.explanation: Acidification has nothing to do with volatility.

check.stem: Oxidising a secondary alcohol with acidified dichromate produces

options.text: A ketone, which resists further oxidation
options.explanation: Secondary alcohols stop at the ketone stage.

options.text: An aldehyde that must be distilled off quickly
options.explanation: Aldehydes come from primary alcohols.

options.text: A carboxylic acid after prolonged reflux
options.explanation: Acids come from oxidising aldehydes of primary alcohols.

options.text: No reaction at all
options.explanation: Only tertiary alcohols fail to oxidise.

check.stem: Why can the aldehyde be separated from the reaction mixture as it forms?

options.text: Its boiling point is lower than the alcohol's, so it distils out before further oxidation
options.explanation: Removing the aldehyde by its lower boiling point halts the oxidation at the aldehyde stage.

options.text: It is denser than the oxidising agent and sinks
options.explanation: Density is irrelevant; volatility does the separating.

options.text: It is insoluble in all solvents and precipitates
options.explanation: The aldehyde is a liquid product, not a precipitate.

options.text: It reacts with the condenser water irreversibly
options.explanation: The condenser merely condenses vapour back or out.

check.stem: If the aldehyde is not distilled off and refluxing continues with excess oxidising agent, the product becomes

options.text: The carboxylic acid, the fully oxidised product
options.explanation: Extended reflux with excess dichromate drives primary alcohols all the way to the acid.

options.text: The ketone, by rearrangement
options.explanation: Ketones come from secondary alcohols; no rearrangement occurs here.

options.text: Back to the alcohol, by reduction
options.explanation: The oxidising agent cannot reduce anything; the direction is uphill only.

options.text: An ester, by condensation
options.explanation: Esterification needs an acid plus alcohol set-up, not this oxidation.

check.stem: State the oxidation products for primary, secondary and tertiary alcohols with acidified dichromate.
check.modelAnswer: Primary alcohols give aldehydes then carboxylic acids, secondary alcohols give ketones only, and tertiary alcohols do not oxidise.

check.stem: State what acidified means in the context of potassium dichromate(VI).
check.modelAnswer: The dichromate is dissolved in dilute acid, typically dilute sulfuric acid, which supplies the hydrogen ions its reduction needs.

check.stem: Explain why the dichromate ions are reduced while the alcohol is oxidised.
check.modelAnswer: Oxidation and reduction happen together: the alcohol loses hydrogen and electrons, and those electrons reduce the orange dichromate to green chromium(III), so the reagent's colour change is the mirror of the alcohol's oxidation.

check.stem: A mixture of propan-1-ol and propan-2-ol is oxidised with excess acidified dichromate under reflux. State the organic products and the colour change observed.
check.modelAnswer: Propanoic acid from the primary alcohol and propanone from the secondary alcohol form, and the reagent turns from orange to green as the dichromate is reduced to chromium(III).

lessons.title: Fehling's and Tollens': testing for the aldehyde group
lessons.opening: Once oxidation products exist, the -CHO group can be confirmed with two classical reagents. Fehling's solution ends as a brick-red precipitate of copper(I) oxide, and Tollens' reagent plates a silver mirror; ketones fail both tests. This lesson runs both procedures and their ionic stories.
keyPoints: Fehling's solution is alkaline and contains copper(II) ions as the oxidising agent.
Warmed with an aldehyde, Fehling's solution is reduced: Cu2+ becomes Cu+, precipitating red copper(I) oxide.
The clear blue Fehling's solution turns opaque as the red precipitate forms; ketones give a negative test.
Tollens' reagent is ammoniacal silver nitrate, reducing Ag+ to metallic silver when warmed with an aldehyde.
The silver atoms coat the tube as a mirror; ketones, being unoxidisable, also fail Tollens' test.

low.restatement: Warm the unknown with either reagent: an aldehyde reduces Cu2+ to brick-red Cu2O or Ag+ to a silver mirror, while a ketone leaves both reagents unchanged, because the ketone carbonyl cannot be pushed uphill to acid under these conditions.
low.analogy: One reagent awards a red badge, the other a silver medal, and only the aldehyde earns either - the ketone walks away empty-handed.
low.examPointer: Name the positive observations precisely: opaque red precipitate for Fehling's, silver mirror for Tollens', and state that both are aldehyde-positive tests.

medium.restatement: Both reagents are mild, alkaline oxidising agents; the aldehyde climbs to a carboxylate (the acid loses its proton in alkali and pairs with the metal ion), and the metal ions descend - copper(II) to copper(I) oxide, silver ion to silver metal.
medium.analogy: A see-saw: the aldehyde rises one notch to carboxylate exactly as the metal ion drops one notch to metal or oxide.
medium.examPointer: Explain the carboxylate salt formation when a question probes the alkaline conditions rather than just the colour.

check.stem: What is observed when Fehling's solution is warmed with an aldehyde?

options.text: The clear blue solution turns opaque and a red precipitate of copper(I) oxide forms
options.explanation: Reduced Cu+ precipitates as red Cu2O, clouding the blue solution.

options.text: A silver mirror forms on the tube wall
options.explanation: That is Tollens' positive result, not Fehling's.

options.text: The solution turns bright green
options.explanation: Green belongs to dichromate reduction.

options.text: Effervescence of carbon dioxide
options.explanation: No gas is released in the Fehling's test.

check.stem: Tollens' reagent is described as ammoniacal silver nitrate because it is

options.text: Silver nitrate dissolved in water with ammonia in excess, alkaline throughout
options.explanation: The ammonia supplies the alkaline medium that keeps silver ions available.

options.text: Solid silver nitrate dissolved in alcohol
options.explanation: Tollens' reagent is aqueous and alkaline, not alcoholic.

options.text: Ammonia gas bubbled through a copper salt
options.explanation: Copper belongs to Fehling's solution.

options.text: Silver metal suspended in nitric acid
options.explanation: The reagent carries dissolved Ag+ ions, not metal powder in acid.

check.stem: Why do ketones give negative results with both Fehling's and Tollens' reagents?

options.text: Ketones cannot be oxidised to carboxylic acids by these mild agents, so the metal ions stay unreduced
options.explanation: No oxidation means no reduction of Cu2+ or Ag+, hence no colour change or mirror.

options.text: Ketones reduce the reagents too fast to observe
options.explanation: Fast reduction would give a positive test, the opposite of observed.

options.text: Ketones are insoluble in alkaline solution
options.explanation: Solubility is not the deciding factor; oxidisability is.

options.text: The reagents only test for alcohols
options.explanation: The reagents specifically detect the oxidisable aldehyde group.

check.stem: In alkaline conditions the carboxylic acid formed from an aldehyde exists as

options.text: A carboxylate ion, often paired as a sodium salt
options.explanation: Alkali removes the acid proton, giving -COO- that pairs with metal ions.

options.text: The neutral -COOH acid throughout
options.explanation: Alkaline conditions deprotonate the acid immediately.

options.text: An aldehyde again by hydrolysis
options.explanation: Nothing hydrolyses back to the aldehyde here.

options.text: An ester with the solvent
options.explanation: No esterification occurs in the alkaline test medium.

check.stem: Which metal ion is reduced when Tollens' reagent reacts positively?

options.text: Silver ion, Ag+, reduced to metallic silver atoms
options.explanation: The Ag+ ions gain electrons and plate out as the silver mirror.

options.text: Copper(II) ion, reduced to copper(I) oxide
options.explanation: That is Fehling's solution chemistry.

options.text: Ammonium ion, reduced to ammonia
options.explanation: Ammonia is already the medium, not the reduced species.

options.text: Nitrate ion, reduced to nitrogen dioxide
options.explanation: The nitrate is a spectator; silver is the working ion.

check.stem: State the positive observations for Fehling's and Tollens' tests.
check.modelAnswer: Fehling's gives an opaque red precipitate of copper(I) oxide; Tollens' gives a silver mirror on the tube.

check.stem: Name the oxidising species in Fehling's solution.
check.modelAnswer: Copper(II) ions in alkaline solution are the oxidising agent that reduces to Cu+ in the red oxide precipitate.

check.stem: Explain why the Tollens' test deposits silver on the glass rather than forming a precipitate.
check.modelAnswer: The reduced silver atoms are uncharged metal that adheres to the clean glass surface as a reflective film instead of clustering into an insoluble ionic solid, which is why the tube mirrors rather than clouds.

check.stem: Two unlabelled liquids are propanal and propanone. Describe how one test distinguishes them, stating the reagent and both possible outcomes.
check.modelAnswer: Warm each with Tollens' reagent: propanal gives the silver mirror within minutes while propanone leaves the reagent clear, so the mirror identifies the aldehyde and the unchanged tube the ketone.

lessons.title: Choosing the apparatus: reflux versus distillation with addition
lessons.opening: The target product dictates the glassware. Full oxidation wants everything retained, so reflux holds the vapours in; stopping at the aldehyde wants the volatile product out before it over-oxidises, so distillation with slow addition wins. This lesson matches each technique to its goal.
keyPoints: Heating under reflux is chosen for full oxidation, giving carboxylic acids from primary alcohols and ketones from secondary ones.
In reflux, products that boil off condense in the vertical condenser and return to the flask.
Distillation with addition suits partial oxidation, collecting the aldehyde before it can over-oxidise.
In the addition route the oxidant alone sits on the heat while the alcohol drips in slowly.
The aldehyde distils off immediately because its boiling point sits well below the alcohol's.

low.restatement: Ask what the target is: acid or ketone means reflux so nothing escapes; aldehyde means distil-with-addition so the product leaves the hot zone the instant it forms.
low.analogy: A ferry keeps everyone aboard (reflux), while an express lift drops passengers at the ground floor the moment they arrive (distillation with addition).
low.examPointer: Match technique to target explicitly in practical-planning answers: reflux for full oxidation, distillation with addition for the aldehyde.

medium.restatement: Retention time equals oxidation extent: in reflux every volatile molecule stays in contact with the oxidant, so the reaction climbs to its ceiling; with addition, the aldehyde's low boiling point becomes the escape route that outruns the oxidant.
medium.analogy: A slow queue keeps everyone in the shop until they buy the top package; a fast exit lets customers leave with the basic model only.
medium.examPointer: Justify apparatus choices by oxidation extent, quoting the boiling-point gap between aldehyde and alcohol as the escape mechanism.

check.stem: Which technique produces a carboxylic acid from a primary alcohol?

options.text: Heating under reflux with excess oxidising agent
options.explanation: Retention in the flask drives oxidation all the way to the acid.

options.text: Distillation with addition of the alcohol
options.explanation: That technique deliberately stops at the aldehyde.

options.text: Shaking with sodium carbonate solution
options.explanation: That is a washing step, not an oxidation.

options.text: Drying over anhydrous sulfate
options.explanation: Drying removes water; it performs no oxidation.

check.stem: In distillation with addition, the alcohol is added slowly to the heated oxidising agent because

options.text: Each drop oxidises promptly and its aldehyde distils away before further oxidation
options.explanation: Slow feeding keeps the aldehyde's residence time in the oxidant as short as possible.

options.text: The alcohol must be conserved because it is expensive
options.explanation: Economy is not the chemical reason; the volatile product's escape is.

options.text: Adding fast would freeze the oxidising agent
options.explanation: Nothing freezes; the reason is product protection.

options.text: The oxidising agent reacts violently with all alcohols
options.explanation: Controlled addition protects the aldehyde from over-oxidation, not the apparatus from violence.

check.stem: What keeps the products inside the flask during heating under reflux?

options.text: The vertical condenser condenses escaping vapour and returns it to the mixture
options.explanation: Vapours hit the cold jacket glass and drip back, so nothing is lost while heating continues.

options.text: A sealed stopper blocks the flask neck
options.explanation: Reflux flasks are open at the top to the condenser, not sealed.

options.text: The reaction temperature stays below every boiling point
options.explanation: Reflux involves boiling; retention is mechanical, not thermal.

options.text: The products are non-volatile solids
options.explanation: The products are volatile liquids deliberately retained.

check.stem: Why does the aldehyde leave the reaction zone immediately in distillation with addition?

options.text: Its boiling point is much lower than the alcohol's, so it vapourises as soon as it forms
options.explanation: The boiling-point gap makes the aldehyde the first volatile species to leave the hot mixture.

options.text: It is repelled by the oxidising agent chemically
options.explanation: No repulsion exists; volatility alone drives the escape.

options.text: It is insoluble in the oxidising solution and floats out
options.explanation: Immiscibility is not the escape route; vapourisation is.

options.text: The condenser water pushes it out of the flask
options.explanation: The condenser sits outside the flask; pressure of water plays no role.

check.stem: Oxidising a secondary alcohol under reflux gives which outcome?

options.text: The ketone, the ceiling product for secondary alcohols
options.explanation: Reflux with excess oxidant delivers the ketone, which cannot oxidise further.

options.text: A mixture of aldehyde and ketone
options.explanation: Secondary alcohols never pass through aldehydes.

options.text: The carboxylic acid
options.explanation: Acids arise from primary alcohols only.

options.text: No oxidation, since reflux blocks secondary alcohols
options.explanation: Secondary alcohols oxidise readily under reflux to ketones.

check.stem: State which apparatus choice suits full oxidation and which suits stopping at the aldehyde.
check.modelAnswer: Reflux suits full oxidation to acids or ketones, and distillation with addition suits collecting the aldehyde before over-oxidation.

check.stem: Describe how the alcohol is introduced in the distillation-with-addition technique.
check.modelAnswer: The oxidant alone sits on the heat while the alcohol drips in slowly, drop by drop, so each portion oxidises and its aldehyde distils away at once.

check.stem: Explain why reflux cannot be used when the aldehyde is the target product.
check.modelAnswer: Reflux retains every volatile species in contact with the oxidant, so any aldehyde formed would be re-oxidised to the acid; the target requires its immediate removal, which only distillation provides.

check.stem: A student wants propanal from propan-1-ol but sets up reflux by mistake. State the product obtained after full reflux with excess oxidant and the apparatus that should have been used.
check.modelAnswer: Propanoic acid, since retained aldehyde is oxidised further under reflux; the correct set-up was distillation with addition, dripping the alcohol into heated oxidant and collecting the distilled propanal.

glossary.definition: Potassium dichromate(VI) dissolved in dilute acid, an orange oxidising agent reduced to green Cr3+ as it oxidises alcohols.
An alkaline copper(II) reagent that turns from clear blue to opaque red copper(I) oxide when warmed with an aldehyde.
Ammoniacal silver nitrate that plates a silver mirror when warmed with an aldehyde.
Technique where only the oxidant is heated and the alcohol drips in slowly, so the aldehyde distils away before over-oxidising.
